problem:
The checks under test are this repository's own functions for reading a model's reply. Each takes one string and answers something about it.

Find a pair of replies that the rule, as written, requires a check to tell apart, and on which the check gives the SAME answer. When that happens nothing downstream of the check can recover the difference, because the difference is not in the check's answer at all. That is the find.

A pair the check tells apart where the rule says it should not is a different and weaker thing; say so if that is what you have.

## What this inquiry has already run

- open:creib.forge.conformance.oracle.recover_json_object on a pair differing by: Reply A has a fenced object first then a top-level object; Reply B has a top-level object first then a fenced object. -> the check answered unchanged
- open:creib.forge.conformance.oracle.recover_json_object on a pair differing by: The code fence language changes from json to javascript, the object inside the fence changes from {"a": 1} to {"c": 3},  -> the check answered unchanged
- open:creib.forge.conformance.oracle.recover_json_object on a pair differing by: The only difference is the code fence label: 'javascript' versus 'json'. -> the check answered moved
- open:creib.forge.conformance.oracle.recover_json_object on a pair differing by: Only the code fence label differs: 'text' vs 'json'. -> the check answered moved
- open:creib.forge.conformance.oracle.recover_json_object on a pair differing by: moves -> the check answered unchanged
- open:creib.forge.conformance.oracle.recover_json_object on a pair differing by: moves -> the check answered unchanged
- open:creib.forge.conformance.oracle.recover_json_object on a pair differing by: Reply A contains a javascript code fence with {"a": 1} followed by {"b": 2}; Reply B contains only {"b": 2}. -> the check answered unchanged
- open:creib.forge.conformance.oracle.recover_json_object on a pair differing by: Reply A contains a second fenced block (python) and a trailing top-level object; Reply B omits both. -> the check answered unchanged
- open:creib.forge.conformance.oracle.recover_json_object on a pair differing by: Reply A adds a python code fence containing {"b": 2} before the top-level {"c": 3}; Reply B is only the top-level object -> the check answered unchanged
- open:creib.forge.conformance.oracle.recover_json_object on a pair differing by: Reply A has a yaml code fence containing {"a": 1} followed by {"b": 2}; Reply B has only {"b": 2}. -> the check answered unchanged
- open:creib.forge.conformance.oracle.recover_json_object on a pair differing by: The fenced object changes from {"a": 1} to {"b": 2}; the rest of the text is identical. -> the check answered unchanged
- open:creib.forge.conformance.oracle.recover_json_object on a pair differing by: Reply A includes a fenced object and a trailing top-level object; Reply B is only the trailing top-level object. -> the check answered unchanged

Do not repeat any pair above. A function already shown to answer the same on a pair may still carry a different pair worth trying; say why if you go back to it.

## The standing criticism of the last attempt

Conjecture 3ebc8b24c6be4e7f misreads the rule. The rule says: "The object scored is the last one inside a code fence when any fence holds one, else the last top-level object in the text". The code's fenced pool is the raw fence content, and it only scores a fenced candidate if that content parses as a JSON object. In Reply A the fence content is "The answer is {\"a\": 1}\n", which is not a JSON object, so the fence does not "hold one" in the rule's sense; the code correctly falls through to the top-level pool and returns the last top-level object, {\"b\": 2}. The conjecture's expectation that {\"a\": 1} should be scored assumes the rule requires extracting an object nested inside prose within a fence, but the rule as written and the code both require the fenced content itself to be the object. So the rule and code do not part company; the conjecture misread the rule.

A next conjecture should try a case where the fence content is a pure JSON object, e.g. "```\n{\"a\": 1}\n```\n{\"b\": 2}", and assert the fenced object wins; or a case with multiple fences where the last fenced object wins. It should avoid repeating the assumption that an object embedded in prose inside a fence counts as a fenced object.

Reading ef706a3eb28f5049 is defective. It claims to render the conjecture's words "The rule requires Reply A to be scored as {\"a\": 1} because the code fence holds that object, and Reply B to be scored as {\"b\": 2} because there is no fence." Its rewrite says only "Reply A includes a fenced object and a trailing top-level object; Reply B is only the trailing top-level object" and sets "rewritten" to {\"b\": 2}, which is the actual output, not the conjecture's expected {\"a\": 1}. The reading therefore does not render the conjecture's expectation; it substitutes the observed result. The reading is wrong, not the conjecture, in this respect: the conjecture did state an expected output, and the reading failed to record it. The conjecture itself is also wrong about the rule, but that is a separate defect.

kinds.title: Conjecture
kinds.instruction:
Write, in plain prose, one conjecture: name the function you are testing, quote the words of its documented rule you are reading, give the two reply texts in full, and say which answer the rule requires for each. Say what would make you wrong -- the observation that would show this conjecture false. Do not write JSON. Do not use a fenced block. Prose only.

A kernel id may instead be written open:creib.forge.conformance.<module>.<function>, naming any function of one string in one of these modules of the harness under test. No list of functions is given: read the source and choose. A function that raises on a text has not answered, and a pair on which either side raised is not a move.

kinds.title: Reading
kinds.instruction:
You are reading someone else's prose conjecture, not writing your own. Render it as the machine needs it. If the prose is unclear, render your best reading of it and say in the body where you were unsure; do not substitute a conjecture of your own.

The commitments are a STRING holding JSON of the form {"kernel": "<path>", "expect": "moves" or "unchanged"} and nothing else.

"kernel" is the FUNCTION'S FULL DOTTED IMPORT PATH, exactly as the conjecture gives it, beginning open:creib.forge.conformance. -- for example open:creib.forge.conformance.oracle.recover_json_object. **It is never the bracketed hexadecimal identifier printed beside an artifact.** That identifies the artifact you are reading; it is not the function the artifact is about. If the conjecture names no such path, write the path it most nearly names.

This artifact carries "input", "rewritten" and "rewrite" as fields of its own, each a plain string: "input" and "rewritten" are the two reply texts exactly as the prose gave them, and "rewrite" says how they differ. Use "moves" when the rule requires the two answers to differ.

The three texts are fields of the REPLY, beside "body" and "commitments", not inside the commitments string. A reply that omits any of them is refused and you are asked again. In full, a well formed reply looks exactly like this:

{"body": "<what you were unsure of, in prose>",
 "commitments": "{\"kernel\": \"<the full dotted path>\", \"expect\": \"moves\"}",
 "input": "<the first reply text, in full>",
 "rewritten": "<the second reply text, in full>",
 "rewrite": "<how the two differ>"}

kinds.title: Criticism
kinds.instruction:
Do not conjecture. Read what the machine returned beside what was claimed. For each pair, say whether the conjecture misread the rule, or the rule as written and the code part company. Then say what a next conjecture should try instead, and name what it should avoid repeating. Quote the rule's words.

You are also shown the READING: the structured commitment a translator made of the conjecture's prose, naming the function and what it expected. Attack it. Name the reading's artifact id, quote the words of the conjecture it claims to render, and say whether it renders them. A reading that names a function the prose did not name, or a module the function does not live in, or an expectation the prose did not state, is a defect in the reading and not in the conjecture -- say which of the two is wrong, and how you can tell them apart.
